recordings.heard: Here's a question. When it's noon in one city, what time is it in a city 300 kilometers to the west? Today, that's easy to answer. But in the early 1800s, it wasn't. Back then, every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun was highest in the sky. That meant noon in one town came a few minutes earlier, or later, than noon in the next town. And for most of history, nobody cared, because nobody could travel fast enough to notice. Then came the railroads. Suddenly, people could pass through several towns in a single hour, and every station kept its own local time. Imagine trying to read a train schedule. In the United States, railroad companies had to deal with dozens of different local times, and mistakes led to missed connections and even accidents. So, in 1883, the railroad companies agreed to divide the country into a small number of time zones. Inside each zone, every clock would show the same time. Some people complained that the railroads were changing the natural time, but the system was so practical that cities quickly adopted it. The following year, an international conference began extending the idea to the rest of the world.

recordings.heard: When you picture an ancient Greek statue, you probably imagine smooth white marble. That image is so familiar that, for centuries, people assumed the Greeks wanted their statues white. They didn't. Most ancient statues were originally painted, often in bright blues, reds, and yellows, with detailed patterns on the clothing and even coloured eyes and lips. So where did the colour go? Well, paint is fragile. After two thousand years of sun, rain and burial in the ground, most of it simply wore away. And here's an uncomfortable detail. When traces of paint did survive, some collectors in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries actually cleaned them off, because by then pure white marble had come to represent classical beauty. In other words, the ancient look we admire is partly a modern creation. How do we know what the originals looked like? Researchers shine ultraviolet light on the stone, which makes invisible traces of pigment glow. They also analyze tiny particles to identify the exact minerals that were used. From that evidence, they've built full-colour reconstructions. Now, many visitors find these reconstructions frankly ugly, too bright, almost like cartoons. But ask yourself whether that reaction tells us about the Greek's taste or about our own. That's a question I'd like you to think about for next week.

Before 1913, it took workers at Henry Ford's factory more than 12 hours to assemble the chassis of one Model T, that's the frame with the engine and wheels. About a year later, it took an hour and a half. What changed? Not the car. What changed was how the work moved. Before, the car stayed in one place and teams of workers walked around it, fetching parts. Ford's engineers turned that around. They put the car on a moving line and had it travel past the workers. Each person stood in one spot and did one small job over and over, maybe tightening the same two bolts all day. The results were dramatic. Because cars were faster to build, they were cheaper to build, and the price of a Model T fell year after year, until ordinary families could afford one. But there was a cost. The work was so dull and so tiring that workers kept quitting, and Ford had to keep hiring and training new ones. His answer in 1914 was the $5 a day, roughly double the usual pay. It worked, people stayed, and as it happened, with wages like that, his own workers could now buy the cars they were building.

I'd like to clear up a misconception before we go any further. When people see photos of a bleached reef, all that ghostly white, they tend to assume they're looking at dead coral. They are not, not yet anyway. Here's what's going on. A coral is an animal, and living inside its tissue are microscopic algae. It's a partnership. The coral provides shelter. and the algae through photosynthesis supply most of the coral's food. They are also what gives a reef its color. Now, when the water stays unusually warm for several weeks, even by just a degree or two, that partnership breaks down. The algae start producing substances that are toxic to their host, and the coral responds by, well, evicting them. What's left is transparent tissue over a white skeleton. Hence bleaching. So a bleached coral is alive, but it's essentially starving. If the water cools in time, the algae come back and the coral recovers. If it doesn't, the coral dies. And this is where I struggle to sound optimistic. A reef can bounce back from one bad summer, but that takes a decade or so. What we're seeing now are heat waves arriving every few years, which simply doesn't leave enough time. So when you read that a reef has recovered, I'd encourage you to ask. Recovered for how long?

By the way, bats aren't blind. That's a myth, eh? But in the dark, they rely on something else, called echolocation. Here's how it works. As a bat flies, it sends out very short, very high calls. Now the insects aren't helpless. Some moths have ears that can pick up bat calls, and when they hear one they dive toward the ground. So next time, we'll look at this contest between the hunter and the hunted.

recordings.heard: Okay, let's start with a little puzzle. In the Sahara, an afternoon can easily reach 40 degrees Celsius, but stay there after dark and the temperature may fall by 20 degrees or more. On a winter night, it can even come close to freezing. Water vapor in the air and clouds overhead absorb the heat and send part of it back down. They work like a blanket. That's why a cloudy night usually feels milder than a clear one. But desert air is extremely dry, and the sky is almost always clear. There's no blanket, so the heat just leaks away into space. And there's a second reason. Sand itself. Sand warms up fast, but only the top layer gets hot, so it doesn't hold much heat. and it loses it quickly once the sun goes down. Compare that with a tropical rainforest. The air there is full of moisture, so the nights are only a little cooler than the days. Same sun, very different nights.

recordings.heard: Picture a pasture that belongs to no one, and is open to every herder in the village. Each herder asks a perfectly reasonable question, should I add one more cow? Well, the profit from that cow is mine alone. The damage it does to the grass, on the other hand, is shared by everybody. So I add the cow. And so does my neighbour and hers. long the pasture is bare. and everyone is worse off. In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin called this the tragedy of the commons, and you can see why the label stuck. Swap the pasture for the open ocean and the cows for fishing boats, and you have a fair description of overfishing. Notice that nobody in the story is a villain. Each person acts sensibly, and together they wreck the thing they depend on. Hardin saw essentially two ways out, divide the resource into private property or have the government regulate it. Now that's where I think he was too gloomy. The political scientist Alina Ostrom spent decades studying real communities, Swiss mountain villages sharing pastures, farmers sharing irrigation water, and she found that many had managed common resources for centuries. They made their own rules, kept an eye on one another, and punished cheats. So the tragedy is a real risk. It just isn't destiny.

recordings.heard: Go down a thousand meters into the ocean, and the last trace of sunlight is gone. You'd expect total darkness. And yet, if you switch off your submarine's lights, the water around you flickers and sparkles. That's bioluminescence. Light made by living things, and down there it's not the exception. What's more interesting is what the light is for. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, and you can guess how that ends for a curious little fish. shrimp do the opposite. When attacked, they spit out a glowing cloud and slip away while the predator is dazzled. Then there's my favorite trick, and for this one we go a little higher, where a faint glow still filters down from the surface. The hatchetfish has lights along its belly. Odd place for them, isn't it? seen from below, a fish is a dark shape against that glow. By lighting its belly to match, the hatchetfish erases its own shadow. It hides by shining. Most of this light is blue, because blue travels farthest through seawater. A few dragonfish, though, make red light, which most of their neighbors can't see at all. In effect, they hunt with a private flashlight.

Okay, so last time we talked about ordinary thunderstorms. Today something much bigger, hurricanes. And I want you to think of a hurricane as an engine. Like any engine, it needs fuel. So what's the fuel? It's warm ocean water. The sea surface has to be at least about 27 degrees Celsius. That's why these storms are born in the tropics, in late summer and early fall, when the ocean is at its warmest. Here's what happens. Warm, wet air rises from the sea surface. As it rises, it cools, and the water vapor in it turns into cloud droplets. Now this is the key step. When vapor turns into liquid, it gives off heat. That heat warms the air around it, so the air rises even faster and more wet air gets pulled in below to replace it. You see, the storm feeds itself. Now why does it spin? That comes from the rotation of the Earth, which bends the path of the moving air. Interestingly, that effect is too weak right at the equator, so hurricanes don't form there. And what stops the engine? Well, take away the fuel. Once a hurricane moves over land or over cooler water, its supply of warm, wet air is cut off, and it gradually weakens.

The most important figure is huge, even though he's standing at the back, and the buildings look as if they might slide off the wall. Now the one on the right, painted about a century later. Suddenly you feel you could walk into the room. So what changed? Painters didn't simply get better at drawing. They learned a system, and we call it linear perspective. The idea is simple. Lines that are parallel in real life, like the edges of a road, seem to come together as they move away from you. In a painting, they meet at a single spot called the Vanishing Point. And the farther away an object is, the smaller you paint it. We usually give the credit to an architect, Filippo Brunelleschi, working in Florence in the early 1400s. He painted a building in his city so accurately that people standing in front of it could compare the two, and they matched. Some years later, another architect, Leon Batista Alberti, wrote the rules down so any painter could learn them. Alberti said a painting should be like an open window. And for the next 400 years or so, that's pretty much what European painting tried to be.

recordings.heard: Let's start with something you've all seen, ice cubes floating in a glass of water. It looks completely ordinary, right? But it's actually strange. With almost every other substance, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks. Drop a piece of solid wax into melted wax, and down it goes. So why is water different? It comes down to the shape of the water molecule and the way these molecules attract one another. In liquid water, the molecules are constantly moving, sliding past each other, and they can crowd fairly close together. But when water freezes, each molecule locks onto its neighbors in a fixed, open pattern, a bit like people holding hands at arm's length. That pattern has a lot of empty space in it. So the same amount of water takes up about 9% more room as ice, which makes ice less dense than the water around it. Now, why should you care? Well, think about a lake in winter. Because ice floats, the lake freezes from the top down, and that layer of ice works like a blanket. The water underneath stays liquid, and fish survive until spring. If ice sank, lakes could freeze solid from the bottom up. Life in cold regions would look very different.

Suppose I gave you the only telephone in the world. What would it be worth to you? Nothing, obviously. There'd be nobody to call. Give a second person a phone, and yours suddenly has some value. Add a million people, and it becomes something you can hardly live without. Economists call this a network effect. A product becomes more valuable to each user user. as the number of users grows. Notice how odd that is. With most goods, it makes no difference to me how many other people own one. My umbrella keeps me just as dry whether or not you have an umbrella too. Now, network effects have a couple of consequences worth remembering. First, getting started is brutally hard. Nobody wants to join an empty network. which is why new platforms so often give their service away for free at the beginning. They're buying a crowd. Second, once a network gets big enough, it tends to pull ahead and stay ahead. A competitor might offer something technically superior and still fail, because what people are really paying for isn't the technology. It's access to everyone else. So, when you hear that a market has ended up with one giant firm, don't assume the best product one. Sometimes it's simply the one that got big first.

recordings.heard: The Iliad runs to more than 15,000 lines, and it took shape before the Greeks were widely using writing. So how on earth did anyone remember it? For a long time, the assumption was that poets simply had extraordinary memories and recited the poem word for word. Then, in the 1930s, a young American scholar named Millman Perry tried something different. Instead of only studying old texts, he traveled to the Balkans, where singers still performed long heroic poems without being able to read, and he recorded them. What he found was that the singers weren't reciting from memory at all. They were composing as they sang. How? They'd absorbed a huge stock of ready-made phrases, each one shaped to fit the rhythm of a line. Think of Homer's swift-footed Achilles or rosy-fingered Don. Readers today may find those repetitions tedious, but for the poet, they were building blocks. Whole scenes like a feast followed familiar patterns, too. And here's the part I find most striking. The singers insisted that they sang a story exactly the same way every time. The recordings showed otherwise. no two performances matched. For them, the same meant the same story, not the same words. So perhaps we should think of an epic less as a fixed text and more as a tradition of performances.

Here's something that might surprise you. If you stand at the top of a very tall building on a windy day, the floor under your feet is moving. Skyscrapers sway. The very tallest can move a meter or more in a storm, and they are designed to. A tower that can bend a little is actually safer than one that can't. So the real problem for engineers isn't keeping the building up. It's keeping the people inside comfortable, because nobody wants to feel seasick at their desk. So how do they do it? One answer is shape. When wind flows around a square tower, it breaks into swirls of air that push the building from side to side. Rounded corners or an outline that changes as the tower rises break up those swirls before they get strong. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai does exactly that. Its outline keeps changing on the way up, so the wind never gets organised. A second answer is weight. Near the top of Taipei 101, in Taiwan, there's an enormous steel ball, more than 600 tons of it, hanging from cables. When the wind pushes the tower one way, the ball swings the other way and absorbs much of the movement. And it isn't hidden. Visitors can go and look at it. For next time, I'd like each of you to find one more building that uses a trick like this.

Today's topic is a farming idea that's thousands of years old and still in use. Crop rotation. The idea is simple. You don't grow the same crop in the same field year after year. Why not? Well, think about what happens if you plant wheat again and again. It takes a lot of nitrogen out of the soil, so each harvest gets a little smaller. and the insects and diseases that, like wheat, stay right there in the field, waiting for next year's meal. Now farmers long ago knew nothing about nitrogen, but they could see the results. In medieval Europe, many villages divided their land into three big fields, and each year one of the three was left empty to rest. It worked, but noticed the cost. A third of the land grew nothing. The real breakthrough, which spread across England in the 1700s, was a four-year rotation. Two of the years were for grain. In the other two, farmers grew turnips and clover. No resting year at all. How was that possible? Clover belongs to the same family as peas and beans. and bacteria living on the roots of these plants take nitrogen from the air and put it back into the soil. So the clover was feeding the field. And the turnips in clover also fed the farm animals through the winter, which meant more animals and more manure for the soil. More food from the same land. Not bad for a simple change of plan.

If you've ever walked out of a city park on a summer evening and felt the air get warmer within a block or two, you've met today's topic in person. It's called the urban heat island effect. Cities tend to be warmer than the countryside around them. It's hardly a new discovery, by the way. An amateur weather watcher named Luke Howard measured it in London some 200 years ago. So why does it happen? Partly it's the materials. Asphalt and dark roofs soak up sunlight all day, and then, crucially, they give that heat back after sunset. That's why the gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night, not at noon, which surprises people. Then there's what's missing. Plants cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves. So when you swap fields for pavement, you lose that free air conditioning. And tall buildings on narrow streets trap warmth that would otherwise escape to the sky. Finally, there's the heat we produce ourselves, from engines and, ironically, from air conditioners. which cool the inside of a building by dumping heat outside. So the hotter a city gets, the more it heats itself. What can planners do? Planting trees and using paler, more reflective surfaces both help. Neither is a miracle cure, but in a heat wave, even a degree or two matters.

Let me start with a slightly depressing fact. Almost nothing that has ever lived became a fossil. When an animal dies, it's normally eaten or it rots, or the weather breaks down its bones. For a fossil to form, a whole chain of unlikely things has to go right. First, the body needs to be buried quickly, say, by mud at the bottom of a lake or by sand in a riverbed. That keeps scavengers away and cuts off oxygen, which slows decay. Even then, the soft parts usually vanish. It's the hard parts, bones, teeth and shells that last. Next, over a very long time. Water moving through the sediment carries dissolved minerals into the tiny spaces inside a bone. Bit by bit, the minerals fill those spaces and may replace the original material. until what's left is, in effect, a copy in stone. And we are not done. That stone has to survive millions of years underground. And then erosion has to bring it back to the surface just when somebody happens to walk by. Now think about what that means for the evidence. Which creatures are we most likely to find? Those with hard parts that lived in or near water. A jellyfish or a bird in a mountain forest, had far worse odds. So the fossil record isn't a photograph of past life. It's more like a guest list with most of the names missing.

We enjoy it in coffee and tea, but the plant makes it to poison insects that chew on its leaves. Now here's the part I find most impressive. Some plants call for help. So how on earth do you find something you can't see? The short answer is, you watch what it does to its surroundings. One approach is to track stars. At the center of our galaxy, astronomers spent years following a handful of stars that whip around an empty-looking point at tremendous speeds. From those orbits, they worked out that the invisible object must have the mass of about four million suns packed into a tiny region. Nothing else we know of fits that description.
